changes.before: Reported QRC gains are difficult to interpret because matched classical controls, multiple random realizations, strong base models, and cross-source validation are rarely combined. We establish a calibrated reproducible matched evaluation workflow on all 22 Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) ADMET endpoints. We compare exactly simulated five-qubit amplitude-encoded reservoirs with real-orthogonal quadratic maps and random Fourier features, using Morgan-ExtraTrees and MapLight-CatBoost. Five scaffold splits and five averaged maps per family control randomness. Ungated QRC is better on 6 and worse on 16 ExtraTrees endpoints, and better on 3 and worse on 19 CatBoost endpoints. After Holm correction, no endpoint is significantly better and three are significantly worse. Gating, joint correction, low-data scaling, finite shots, simulated noise, and a bounded reservoir-family search do not produce a cross-base advantage. External validation is source-dependent: CatBoost improves by 0.040 AUROC on 293 non-overlapping hERG molecules but both bases degrade on 2,317 B3DB BBB molecules. The hERG difference combines a QRC gain and an orthogonal-branch decrement relative to the base. Continuous-label ranking and an independent pIC50 regression do not survive joint multiplicity correction. Known-signal calibration recovered QRC and classical targets, with null false-positive rates of 2.0-4.7%. A Qiskit/Aer audit preserved rank under errors but attenuated amplitudes. Chemical-space analyses show no simple source effect. The main contribution is a calibrated evaluation workflow. The conclusion is bounded by five-qubit amplitude encoding, 15 Pauli readouts, a linear residual head, and exact state-vector simulation; it is not a general claim against other encodings, trainable circuits, larger reservoirs, or physical hardware.
changes.after: Reported QRC gains are difficult to compare because studies often differ in classical controls, random realizations, base-model strength, and external validation. We evaluated this question under a common, calibrated protocol across all 22 Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) ADMET endpoints. We compared exact simulations of five-qubit amplitude-encoded reservoirs with real-orthogonal quadratic maps and random Fourier features, using Morgan-ExtraTrees and MapLight-CatBoost. Five scaffold splits and five averaged maps per family quantified randomness. Ungated QRC was better on 6 and worse on 16 ExtraTrees endpoints, and better on 3 and worse on 19 CatBoost endpoints. After Holm correction, no endpoint was significantly better and three were significantly worse. Validation gating, joint QRC-orthogonal residuals, low-data scaling, finite shots, simulated noise, and a bounded reservoir-family search did not produce a cross-base advantage. External validation was source-dependent: CatBoost improved by 0.040 AUROC on 293 non-overlapping hERG molecules, whereas both bases degraded on 2,317 B3DB BBB molecules. The hERG difference combined a QRC gain with an orthogonal-branch decrement relative to the base. Continuous-label ranking and an independent pIC50 regression did not survive joint multiplicity correction. Known-signal calibration recovered QRC and classical targets, with null false-positive rates of 2.0-4.7%. Circuit-level simulation preserved rank under error but attenuated amplitudes. Chemical-space analyses showed no simple source effect. The main contribution is a calibrated evaluation workflow; its scope is limited to five-qubit amplitude encoding, 15 Pauli readouts, a linear residual head, and exact state-vector simulation, not to other encodings, trainable circuits, larger reservoirs, or physical hardware.

The value of quantum features therefore cannot be inferred from a comparison with a single weak base model.

changes.before: We ask a bounded question. Under the same input, the same 15 readouts, and the same linear residual head, does a fixed five-qubit reservoir provide an increment relative to real-orthogonal quadratic maps and random Fourier features across the 22 TDC endpoints, two classical bases, and independent external sources? Figure 1 summarizes the design. The study makes three contributions. First, it formalizes the current QRC and linear residual head as a constrained real quadratic feature family and constructs an equal-input, equal-capacity, equal-map-budget quadratic control. Second, it evaluates the family across all 22 endpoints with validation gating and multiple-testing correction. Third, it uses low-data, finite-shot, simulated-noise, bounded-family, two-source external, continuous-label, independent pIC50 regression, and chemical-space analyses to delimit the conclusion.
changes.after: The study addresses one question: with molecular input, 15 readouts, and the linear residual head held constant, does a fixed five-qubit reservoir add predictive value beyond real-orthogonal quadratic maps and random Fourier features across 22 TDC endpoints, two classical bases, and independent external sources? Figure 1 summarizes the design. The study makes three contributions. First, it treats the current QRC residual as a constrained real quadratic feature family and constructs a control with the same input, readout dimension, fitted-parameter budget, and map budget. Second, it evaluates the family across all 22 endpoints with validation gating and multiple-testing correction. Third, it uses low-data, finite-shot, simulated-noise, bounded-family, two-source external, continuous-label, independent pIC50 regression, and chemical-space analyses to define the limits of the conclusion.
changes.reason: Converted a broad statement of scope into one research question and three explicit, non-overlapping contributions.

changes.location: 3 Data, Splits, and Statistical Evaluation, paragraph 3
changes.before: The primary effect was computed from unrounded predictions by scoring each seed and then averaging the five seeds. For AUROC, AUPRC, and Spearman, the effect is the new method minus the reference; for MAE, it is the reference minus the new method; positive values always indicate improvement. We used 1,000 paired scaffold bootstrap resamples for 95% intervals and 1,999 paired scaffold permutations for the primary tests, followed by Holm correction across the 22 endpoints [18-20]. Exploratory TOST analysis used a practical margin of 0.01 for AUROC, AUPRC, and Spearman and 2% of base MAE for MAE. These margins are benchmark interpretation thresholds, not clinical limits. TOST consists of two one-sided tests. We describe practical equivalence only when the 90% confidence interval lies inside the prespecified margin and the equivalence test is significant after Holm correction. Results are reported in three states: a Holm-significant negative difference indicates significant degradation, a Holm-significant positive difference indicates improvement, and a significant equivalence test indicates practical statistical equivalence; all other cases are unresolved. Equivalence does not imply identical mechanisms or identical per-molecule predictions.
changes.after: The primary effect was computed from unrounded predictions: each seed was scored, and the scores were averaged over the five seeds. For AUROC, AUPRC, and Spearman, the effect is the new method minus the reference; for MAE, it is the reference minus the new method. Positive values indicate improvement. We used 1,000 paired scaffold bootstrap resamples for 95% intervals and 1,999 paired scaffold permutations for the primary tests, with Holm correction across the 22 endpoints [18-20].

changes.location: 4.2 Five-Qubit Reservoir and Matched Classical Features, paragraph 2
changes.before: Five qubits support 32 real amplitudes, so the 32-dimensional PCA is the smallest complete amplitude input without truncation or padding at this scale. For normalized PCA vector v, the amplitudes are a_j = v_j / ||v||. The Hamiltonian H and evolution U = exp(-iHt) are fixed and not trained on test labels. changes.location: 4.2 Five-Qubit Reservoir and Matched Classical Features, Proposition 1
changes.before: Proposition 1. For any fixed set of 15 diagonal Pauli observables D_j and any fixed unitary U, the readouts of a normalized 32-dimensional real input a satisfy q_j(a)=a^T A_j a, where A_j=Re(U^dagger D_j U). Therefore any intercept-free linear readout is a real quadratic form a^T M a+b: fixed five-qubit QRC with a linear residual head belongs to a model family constrained by at most 15 real quadratic forms. The proof follows by expanding (Ua)^dagger D_j (Ua). This does not make QRC equivalent to a particular real-orthogonal map; it defines the function class available under the current encoding and readout.
changes.after: Proposition 1. For any fixed set of 15 diagonal Pauli observables D_j and any fixed unitary U, the readouts of a normalized 32-dimensional real input a satisfy q_j(a)=a^T A_j a, where A_j=Re(U^dagger D_j U). An intercept can be absorbed into b, so any linear readout of these features has the form a^T M a+b. Thus fixed five-qubit QRC with a linear residual head belongs to a model family constrained by at most 15 real quadratic forms. The proof follows by expanding (Ua)^dagger D_j(Ua). This class description does not equate QRC with a particular real-orthogonal map; it identifies the function family and motivates the matched control.
changes.reason: Removed the contradiction between 'intercept-free' and the intercept-containing expression, and stated the role of the proposition directly.

changes.location: 6.1 What the Constrained Quadratic Map Explains, paragraph 1
changes.before: With real amplitude inputs, every Z or ZZ expectation after fixed evolution can be computed exactly as a real symmetric quadratic form. Training-side standardization is an affine feature transform, so the linear readout only combines these quadratic forms and adds a fixed offset. This structure applies to the normalized 32-dimensional latent input, not to the raw molecular graph. changes.after: With real amplitude inputs, every Z or ZZ expectation after fixed evolution is a real symmetric quadratic form. Training-side standardization is affine, so the linear readout combines these forms and adds a fixed offset. Given the fitted parameters, the QRC residual can be reproduced by a real quadratic form and a constant on the normalized 32-dimensional latent input. This statement applies to that latent space, not to the raw molecular graph. All five QRC readout matrices had rank 15 and a median condition number of 1.210; the real-orthogonal readout matrices had rank 15 and condition number 1.000. On held-out molecular features, effective rank was 14.10 versus 14.62 on ExtraTrees and 12.82 versus 14.25 on CatBoost, with linear centered-kernel alignments of 0.20 and 0.30. The branches had equal output and fitted-parameter budgets, different geometry, and comparable but not identical effective feature capacity.
changes.reason: Distinguished full-rank readout matrices from held-out feature effective rank and removed the unsupported phrase that nominal capacities were equal.

changes.location: 6.3 What the Strong Base and External Cohorts Reveal, paragraph 1
changes.before: The strong-base experiment is the main difference from the preliminary pilot. MapLight-CatBoost outperformed Morgan-ExtraTrees on 21/22 endpoints, while the relative advantage of QRC did not persist on the stronger base. Joint gating did not produce a stable increment across endpoints, and finite-shot, low-data, and simulated-noise analyses did not reverse this result. The positive external hERG signal suggests that a source-specific candidate may remain. Its pIC50 rank transfer and independent continuous regression point in the same weak direction, but the rank transfer did not survive 12-comparison Holm correction and the regression confidence intervals crossed zero without any corrected significant contrast. Circuit-level Aer errors produced strong readout attenuation but retained high feature-ranking correlations, without adding advantage evidence. BBB logBB transfer was near zero, and significant B3DB BBB classification degradation rules out a cross-source interpretation. Future quantum encodings should be tested directly on a strong base with matched input, capacity, and candidate budgets. For computer-aided molecular design practice, fixed amplitude-encoded QRC should not yet be treated as a general ADMET descriptor; new quantum encodings should also be evaluated on genuinely independent regression cohorts and source cohorts.
changes.after: The strong-base comparison provides a direct stress test. MapLight-CatBoost outperformed Morgan-ExtraTrees on 21/22 endpoints, but QRC's relative advantage did not persist on the stronger base. Validation gating, finite shots, low-data scaling, and simulated noise did not reveal a transferable quantum correction. The circuit audit likewise showed readout attenuation without new advantage evidence.
changes.reason: Deleted an undefined comparison with a preliminary pilot and stated the role of the strong base directly.

changes.before: We added a descriptive chemical-space audit to determine whether the external cohort differences could be attributed to source proximity. Both cohorts were already free of exact canonical identities from their corresponding TDC archive. For hERG, 23 of 293 molecules (7.8%) retained a Bemis-Murcko scaffold present in TDC train/validation data; the median nearest Morgan Tanimoto similarity (radius 2, 2048 bits) to TDC train/validation molecules was 0.234 and the 90th percentile was 0.423. For B3DB BBB, 562 of 2,317 molecules (24.3%) shared a TDC train/validation scaffold, with a median nearest similarity of 0.346 and a 90th percentile of 0.722. B3DB contained 48.9% positives versus 76.4% in the full TDC BBB archive, whereas hERG contained 76.4% positives versus 68.9% in TDC. The two cohorts therefore differ from their TDC sources in both chemical proximity and label composition.

Both cohorts were free of exact canonical identities from the corresponding TDC archive. For B3DB BBB, 562 of 2,317 molecules (24.3%) shared a TDC train/validation scaffold, with a median nearest similarity of 0.346 and a 90th percentile of 0.722. B3DB contained 48.9% positives versus 76.4% in the full TDC BBB archive, whereas hERG contained 76.4% versus 68.9% in TDC. The two cohorts differed from their TDC sources in both chemical proximity and label composition.
changes.reason: Replaced an unnecessary description of the authors' action with a direct statement of what the analysis tested.

changes.before: Re-scoring the existing held-out predictions by these chemical strata did not support a simple scaffold-overlap explanation for the hERG signal. For CatBoost, the hERG gated-QRC minus gated-orthogonal effect was -0.0026 AUROC among the 23 molecules with a shared train/validation scaffold and +0.0452 among the 270 molecules with a novel scaffold. The effect was +0.0196 in the highest nearest-similarity quartile and +0.0494 in the remaining three quartiles. In contrast, the BBB effect was negative across shared-scaffold, novel-scaffold, and similarity strata. Full source audits and hERG strata are reported in Supplementary Tables S5 and S6. These descriptive strata locate where an effect appears; they do not control source, assay batch, or label definition and cannot establish a causal chemical mechanism.
changes.after: Stratifying the held-out predictions did not support a simple scaffold-overlap or similarity explanation for the hERG signal. For CatBoost, the hERG gated-QRC minus gated-orthogonal effect was -0.0026 AUROC among the 23 molecules with a shared train/validation scaffold and +0.0452 among the 270 molecules with a novel scaffold. The earlier top-quartile split gave +0.0196 in the highest-similarity group and +0.0494 in the other three quartiles. The finer quartile analysis was non-monotonic: CatBoost and ExtraTrees were positive in Q3 but not in every adjacent quartile. B3DB effects were negative across shared-scaffold, novel-scaffold, and most similarity strata. Full source audits are reported in Supplementary Tables S5, S6, and S16. These descriptive strata locate where an effect appears; they do not control source, assay batch, or label definition and cannot establish a causal chemical mechanism.
changes.reason: Aligned the discussion with the expanded quartile analysis and removed wording that suggested a monotonic source gradient.

changes.before: The hERG point improvement is a candidate signal, not evidence that the quantum features learned a mechanism of cardiac toxicity. The significant B3DB negative transfer is not evidence that quantum methods are universally ineffective for ADMET. The QML-ADMET studies reviewed here use different fixed reservoirs, Hamiltonian-derived features, quantum-inspired preprocessing, circuit search, or jointly trained residuals; their task counts, controls, and external validation settings do not support a like-for-like equivalence claim. Table 1 summarizes the main differences and Supplementary Table S4 provides the expanded comparison. The contribution is a reusable minimum evaluation workflow: prespecify the primary comparator, match candidate and map budgets, infer with scaffold clusters, correct across endpoints, interpret equivalence separately from superiority, and report both cross-base and cross-source results.
changes.after: Neither the hERG candidate nor the B3DB negative transfer establishes a mechanistic or general quantum effect. The reviewed QML-ADMET studies use different fixed reservoirs, Hamiltonian-derived features, quantum-inspired preprocessing, circuit search, or jointly trained residuals. Their task counts, controls, and external validation settings do not support like-for-like equivalence. Table 1 summarizes the design differences, and Supplementary Table S4 provides the expanded comparison. The study contributes a reusable minimum evaluation protocol: prespecify the primary comparator, match candidate and map budgets, infer with scaffold clusters, correct across endpoints, interpret equivalence separately from superiority, and report both cross-base and cross-source results.
changes.reason: Combined the two broad negative statements into one bounded interpretation and kept the literature differences connected to the evaluation protocol.

changes.before: The fixed official test set supports reproducible comparisons but may have been reused by earlier public leaderboards and is not a prospective cohort. Similar molecules may remain under different Murcko scaffolds, so extrapolation across laboratories, time, and chemical series requires separate evaluation. The exact state-vector calculation is a controlled choice for isolating circuit expressivity and does not replace evaluation of physical gate error, readout crosstalk, connectivity, or scheduling. The equivalence margins are exploratory and are not clinical or regulatory thresholds [3-5,21].
changes.after: Three evaluation limits constrain generalization. The public TDC test sets may have been reused by earlier studies and are not prospective cohorts; scaffold splits reduce, but do not eliminate, near analogues across laboratories, time, and chemical series. The low-data analysis covers eight endpoints, and its 96-record minimum changes the effective fraction for the smallest endpoints. The primary external comparison contains two classification cohorts that differ in assay source and label construction [3-5].
changes.reason: Grouped related evaluation limitations and placed the non-clinical equivalence caveat with the statistical scope.

changes.before: We evaluate independent per-molecule inputs and one fixed five-qubit evolution. Finite-shot analysis sampled each Pauli expectation independently; noise analysis used a simplified local depolarizing model and did not simulate gate error, leakage, readout crosstalk, or measurement scheduling. The supplementary Qiskit/Aer audit includes transpiled gate depolarization and readout flips, but still uses fixed synthetic error parameters, omits drift, crosstalk, hardware connectivity, and physical scheduling, and does not retrain the full predictor on circuit-noisy features. We did not test trainable circuits, task-conditioned amplitude encoding, or other PCA dimensions. The low-data analysis covers eight representative endpoints, and the 96-record minimum changes the effective fraction for the smallest endpoints. The primary external analysis contains two classification endpoints; hERG uses the source-defined binary cutoff but still differs in assay source and label generation. The supplementary continuous-label analysis ranks binary-model outputs and is not an independently trained regression evaluation. The separate pIC50 regression uses 214 test molecules in 155 scaffolds under a fixed protocol; it is scaffold-disjoint but statistically underpowered. B3DB logBB was available for only 613/2,317 non-overlapping molecules and was strongly class-enriched, so it does not represent the full BBB chemical space. The chemical-space figure uses a linear fingerprint projection and three basic descriptors, not a complete applicability-domain model, and equivalence counts depend on the prespecified margins. Random-map sensitivity covers five realizations per family, and hardware cost, decoherence, and connectivity were not evaluated on physical devices. The present comparison therefore applies only to five-qubit amplitude encoding, a fixed Hamiltonian reservoir, 15 Pauli readouts, a linear residual head, and exact simulation. It does not establish the behavior of other quantum representations or physical hardware. Repeated use of the public TDC test set may also reduce generalization to unseen chemical series.
changes.after: The execution boundary is equally explicit. Exact state-vector calculation isolates the fixed circuit's expressive behavior but does not evaluate physical gate error, readout crosstalk, connectivity, or scheduling. Finite-shot analysis samples each Pauli expectation independently. The simplified depolarizing model omits gate-specific error, leakage, crosstalk, and physical scheduling. The Qiskit/Aer audit adds transpiled gate depolarization and readout flips, but uses fixed synthetic error parameters and does not retrain the full predictor on circuit-noisy features. Trainable circuits, task-conditioned amplitude encoding, and other PCA dimensions were not evaluated.
changes.reason: Removed repeated broad negatives and retained each real hardware or circuit omission once.

changes.before: Across 22 official TDC ADMET endpoints, fixed five-qubit reservoir residuals showed no stable increment over equal-capacity real-orthogonal quadratic maps. This result held on both Morgan-ExtraTrees and the stronger MapLight-CatBoost base. Validation gating pushed some harmful residuals back to the classical base but did not produce a stable advantage over the gated classical control. Joint gating, low-data scaling, finite shots, and simulated decoherence did not reverse this conclusion. External hERG provided a CatBoost-specific candidate signal, whereas B3DB BBB showed significant negative transfer. Continuous-label rank transfer and independent pIC50 regression both showed only uncorrected weak CatBoost/hERG directions, with no Holm-significant comparison and no corresponding BBB signal. The circuit-level audit showed high rank preservation under low and medium errors but marked readout attenuation and no new advantage evidence. Chemical-space and physicochemical strata support a source-dependent local signal rather than an identifiable general chemical rule. The main contribution is a reproducible QML evaluation workflow. The result is bounded by the tested five-qubit amplitude-encoded, fixed-Hamiltonian reservoir with 15 Pauli readouts, a linear residual head, and exact simulation; other encodings, trainable circuits, larger reservoirs, and physical hardware require independent evaluation.
changes.after: Across 22 official TDC ADMET endpoints, fixed five-qubit reservoir residuals showed no stable increment over real-orthogonal quadratic maps with the same readout dimension, fitted-parameter budget, and map budget. This result held on both Morgan-ExtraTrees and the stronger MapLight-CatBoost base. Validation gating reduced harmful residuals but did not produce a stable advantage over gated classical controls. Joint gating, low-data scaling, finite shots, and simulated decoherence did not reverse the result. External hERG produced a CatBoost-specific candidate signal, whereas B3DB BBB showed significant negative transfer. Continuous-label transfer and independent pIC50 regression showed only uncorrected weak CatBoost/hERG directions, and neither had a corresponding BBB signal. Known-signal calibration recovered the synthetic QRC and classical targets, and null false-positive rates remained at or below 5%.
changes.reason: Converted a single dense paragraph into an evidence summary that does not repeat the full limitations list.

insertions.location: 3 Data, Splits, and Statistical Evaluation, paragraph 3
insertions.text: Exploratory TOST used margins of 0.01 for AUROC, AUPRC, and Spearman and 2% of base MAE for MAE. These thresholds define practical benchmark equivalence, not clinical limits. Practical equivalence was reported only when the 90% confidence interval lay inside the prespecified margin and the equivalence test remained significant after Holm correction. Results are classified as significant degradation, significant improvement, practical equivalence, or unresolved. Equivalence does not imply identical mechanisms or identical per-molecule predictions.
insertions.purpose: Separated hypothesis testing from TOST interpretation.

insertions.text: The continuous-label rank transfer produced an unadjusted CatBoost/hERG pIC50 Spearman difference of +0.043. This difference did not survive Holm correction across 12 comparisons and did not replicate for BBB logBB. Because it ranks predictions from binary-trained models, it is not an independently trained regression evaluation; the B3DB continuous subset is 86.8% positive.
insertions.purpose: Separated external effect decomposition from continuous-label transfer.
Separated an unrelated audit from continuous regression.

insertions.text: We also examined circuit-specific readout degradation with explicit Qiskit circuits: 32-dimensional amplitude preparation, an eight-step Lie-Trotter fixed-Hamiltonian evolution, and all-qubit Z-basis measurement. The panel covered eight representative endpoints, 32 stratified test states per endpoint, and five reservoir maps; transpiled circuits had depth 81 and about 136 operations. Aer density-matrix simulation included one- and two-qubit gate depolarizing errors plus independent readout flips.
insertions.purpose: Placed circuit design before its results.

insertions.text: Relative to exact matrix readouts, normalized RMSE was 0.189-0.199, 0.337-0.351, and 0.551-0.569 at low, medium, and high error, respectively. Signal slopes were approximately 0.81, 0.66, and 0.45, whereas Spearman correlations remained 0.9974-0.9986, 0.9916-0.9958, and 0.9742-0.9866. The noiseless Trotterized RMSE was 0.0058-0.0070. Circuit errors mainly contracted readout amplitude while retaining substantial relative ordering; they did not add new advantage evidence. This is a readout-fidelity audit, not end-to-end retraining on noisy features. Full results are reported in Supplementary Figure S5 and Supplementary Table S11.
insertions.purpose: Made circuit evidence and its interpretation contiguous.

insertions.location: 5.10 Benchmark Calibration and Source Diagnostics, paragraph 4
insertions.text: External stratification did not follow a monotonic similarity gradient. For CatBoost/hERG, QRC-specific AUROC changed from +0.003 in Q1 to +0.037, +0.070, and +0.013 across Q2-Q4; the Q3 interval [+0.011, +0.128] excluded zero. ExtraTrees showed a different pattern, with QRC-specific effects of -0.064, -0.059, +0.055, and -0.006 across Q1-Q4; the Q3 interval was [+0.018, +0.092]. B3DB showed no consistently positive quartile. The hERG signal was localized and source-specific rather than a simple function of nearest-TDC similarity.
insertions.purpose: Connected the source-dependence claim to non-monotonic quartile evidence.

insertions.location: 6.3 What the Strong Base and External Cohorts Reveal, paragraph 2
insertions.text: The external results support only a source-specific candidate on hERG. The same direction appeared in pIC50 rank transfer and independent regression, but neither survived the joint multiplicity correction. B3DB logBB was near zero and B3DB BBB classification degraded significantly, so the hERG result cannot be generalized across sources. These findings support testing future quantum encodings on a strong classical base with matched input, capacity, and candidate budgets; they do not establish a general ADMET descriptor.
insertions.purpose: Separated the evidence summary from the design implication and removed repeated scope language.
Separated interpretation boundaries from the chemical-space description.

insertions.text: The auxiliary analyses have narrower scope. Continuous-label transfer ranks outputs from binary-trained models and is not an independently trained regression. The separate pIC50 regression uses 214 test molecules in 155 scaffolds under a fixed protocol and has limited statistical power. B3DB logBB was available for only 613/2,317 non-overlapping molecules and was strongly class-enriched. The chemical-space figure uses a linear fingerprint projection and three basic descriptors, not a complete applicability-domain model, and TOST margins are exploratory benchmark thresholds rather than clinical or regulatory limits [21]. Random-map sensitivity covers five realizations per family. The known-signal calibration uses synthetic targets drawn from the tested feature families; it establishes detectability for those designs, not coverage of every possible nonlinear signal. The reported comparison applies to five-qubit amplitude encoding, a fixed Hamiltonian reservoir, 15 Pauli readouts, a linear residual head, and exact simulation; other encodings, trainable circuits, larger reservoirs, and physical hardware require independent evaluation.
insertions.purpose: Consolidated auxiliary-analysis limits and stated the final scope once.

insertions.text: The study's main contribution is a calibrated matched-evaluation workflow that distinguishes ordinary quadratic effects, reservoir-specific candidate effects, and source dependence. The hERG signal is a bounded candidate, not a demonstrated mechanism of cardiotoxicity, and the B3DB result does not show that quantum methods are universally ineffective. The conclusion applies to the tested five-qubit amplitude-encoded, fixed-Hamiltonian reservoir with 15 Pauli readouts, a linear residual head, and exact simulation; other encodings, trainable circuits, larger reservoirs, and physical hardware require independent evaluation.
